content: The American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS) is an organization dedicated to fostering collaboration among scientists, safeguarding scientific freedom, promoting scientific responsibility, and advancing science education and outreach for the benefit of humanity. It is recognized as the largest general scientific society in the world and is the publisher of the prestigious journal Science. The AAAS was established on September 20, 1848, in Pennsylvania as a reformation of the Association of American Geologists and Naturalists. William C. Redfield was elected as the first president due to his comprehensive plans for the organization. The initial constitution, adopted at the founding meeting, outlined the society's mission to promote scientific dialogue and collaboration, thereby enhancing the efficiency of scientific endeavors and accelerating progress. The organization also aimed to expand resources available to the scientific community through active advocacy. At its inception, the AAAS had only 87 members, including Matthew Fontaine Maury, who presented a detailed scientific report on his Wind and Current Charts during the first meeting. Maury emphasized the importance of simultaneous observations and proposed international cooperation to improve his work, suggesting that navies from various nations could contribute their logbooks and sea journals to the United States Naval Observatory. William Barton Rogers, a professor at the University of Virginia and later the founder of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, proposed a resolution to seek support from the U.S. Navy for Maury’s efforts. This resolution was adopted, and a committee of prominent scientists, including Joseph Henry, Benjamin Peirce, James H. Coffin, and Stephen Alexander, was formed to address the matter. This marked an early example of scientific cooperation within the AAAS. By 1860, the organization had grown to over 2,000 members. However, the American Civil War interrupted its activities, and the AAAS became dormant after its August 1861 meeting in Nashville, Tennessee, was indefinitely postponed. The organization was revived in 1866 under the leadership of Frederick Barnard, and it resumed its growth, although the emergence of other specialized scientific societies limited its expansion. Unlike the National Academy of Sciences (NAS), which elects its members, the AAAS allowed anyone to join, regardless of scientific credentials, while granting the title of Fellow of the AAAS to distinguished scientists. The AAAS has engaged in various activities, such as using satellite imagery in 2007 to document human rights abuses in Burma. Its governance is structured around four entities: the Office of the President, the Administrative Officers, the Council, and the Board of Directors. The presidency of the AAAS is a three-year term, with the individual serving as President-elect in the first year, President in the second year, and Chairperson of the Board of Directors in the third year. The current president, David Baltimore, is a Nobel laureate and a professor at the California Institute of Technology. He became president in February 2007 and will transition to Chairperson of the Board in February 2008. His successor, James J. McCarthy, a professor at Harvard University, will assume the presidency in February 2008. Past presidents of the AAAS include notable figures such as John Wesley Powell, Edward Charles Pickering, Margaret Mead, and Stephen Jay Gould. The AAAS employs three categories of high-level administrative officers: The organization is divided into 24 sections, each focusing on a specific scientific discipline or area of interest, ranging from agriculture and astronomy to neuroscience and the social impact of science. Additionally, the AAAS has 262 affiliate societies and academies of science, representing over 10 million members worldwide. The Council of the AAAS consists of the Board of Directors, retiring section chairpersons, and elected delegates, including representatives from the National Academy of Sciences and various regions of the country. The Council meets annually to oversee the Association's activities, elect new Fellows, propose constitutional amendments, and establish new scientific sections. The President of the AAAS serves as the Chairperson of the Council, and members serve three-year terms. The Board of Directors includes the Chairperson, the President, the President-elect, eight elected Directors, the Executive Officer, and up to two additional appointed Directors. Members of the Board serve four-year terms, except for appointed Directors, who serve three-year terms. The Board is responsible for managing the Association's funds, publishing budgets, appointing administrators, proposing amendments, and determining the timing and location of national meetings. It also has the authority to speak publicly on behalf of the Association and must maintain regular communication with the Council to coordinate actions. The current Chairperson of the Board is John P. Holdren, a professor at Harvard University and director of the Woods Hole Research Center. He will serve in this role until February 2008.
